defaults.permitted_development: A garden room can usually be permitted development in England where it remains an incidental outbuilding to the house, stays behind the principal elevation, remains single storey and complies with the Class E height and coverage limits. It should not operate as a separate dwelling or a self-contained residential suite.

rules.height_rules: Keep the room single storey with eaves no higher than 2.5m. The overall height limit is 4m for a dual-pitched roof, 3m for any other roof and 2.5m overall if any part sits within 2m of a boundary.
rules.depth_rules: There is no separate garden-room depth allowance. The key tests are curtilage position, staying behind the principal elevation and keeping additions and outbuildings within 50% of the land around the original house.
rules.boundary_rules: Any part within 2m of a boundary is limited to 2.5m overall. On designated land, side garden-room siting can need permission, and listed-building curtilages need extra caution before relying on permitted development.
rules.roof_rules: A simple single-storey roof is the safest route. A dual-pitched roof can reach 4m and other roofs 3m, but boundary siting can reduce that to 2.5m overall. Raised platforms, balconies and veranda-style features are outside the ordinary Class E route.
rules.materials_rules: Glazing and modern cladding can be acceptable, but the room should still look subordinate to the dwellinghouse and remain incidental in use. A fit-out that reads like a separate bedroom, bathroom and kitchen suite is more likely to need permission.

rules.permitted_development: A modest garden room is often treated as an outbuilding under the normal householder rules, provided it stays incidental to the dwellinghouse and within the usual siting, height and 50% coverage limits. It should not be laid out as separate living accommodation.

rules.height_rules: The usual benchmark is single storey only, eaves up to 2.5m, 4m overall for a dual-pitched roof and 3m for another roof form. Any part within 2m of the boundary brings the overall cap down to 2.5m.
rules.depth_rules: Garden rooms do not have an independent depth rule like extensions. What matters is curtilage location, staying behind the principal elevation and keeping overall coverage by additions and outbuildings within the normal 50% limit.
rules.boundary_rules: Most garden-room boundary issues come from height and prominence. Anything within 2m of the boundary is limited to 2.5m overall, and designated land adds extra limits for side-garden positions and some structures set more than 20m from the house.
rules.roof_rules: Keep the roof simple and subordinate. Dual-pitched forms can go up to 4m, other roofs up to 3m, but boundary siting can reduce the overall cap to 2.5m. Roof terraces and raised platforms are outside the normal outbuilding right.
rules.materials_rules: The external finish should look deliberate and subordinate rather than like a second home in the garden. However modern the design is, the room should remain incidental in use and not function as self-contained living space.

rules.permitted_development: Garden rooms can usually use the outbuilding rules where they remain single storey, subordinate to the house and incidental in use. Once the space starts operating like an annexe or separate unit, planning permission is much more likely to be needed.

rules.height_rules: Keep the room within the standard outbuilding limits: single storey, eaves no more than 2.5m, a 4m overall maximum for a dual-pitched roof and 3m for other roofs, or 2.5m overall if it sits within 2m of a boundary.
rules.depth_rules: Instead of a fixed projection limit, the real garden-room checks are position within the curtilage, not building forward of the principal elevation and not pushing total site coverage beyond the usual 50% allowance.
rules.boundary_rules: If the room is close to a boundary, design around the 2.5m overall cap. Also allow for tighter designated-land controls where the building sits at the side of the house or well away from it.
rules.roof_rules: A modest single-storey roof is usually easiest to keep lawful. Dual-pitched roofs can reach 4m and others 3m, though close boundary siting reduces the overall limit to 2.5m, and raised platforms or terrace-style designs are not part of the usual right.
rules.materials_rules: Materials can be contemporary, but the room should still read as a domestic ancillary structure tied to the house. Avoid servicing, layouts or internal fit-out that would make it behave like a separate annexe.

rules.permitted_development: A garden room can often stay within householder permitted development if it remains incidental to the house, sits behind the principal elevation and fits the outbuilding height and coverage limits. That route is for a home office, studio or gym-type use, not a self-contained annexe.

rules.height_rules: Use the normal outbuilding height envelope: single storey only, eaves no higher than 2.5m, up to 4m overall with a dual-pitched roof or 3m with any other roof, falling to 2.5m overall within 2m of a boundary.
rules.depth_rules: There is no separate garden-room depth allowance. The key tests are whether it stays within the residential curtilage, remains behind the principal elevation and keeps the total area taken by additions and outbuildings within 50% of the land around the original house.
rules.boundary_rules: Boundary siting is often what decides the design. Within 2m of a boundary the overall height must stay at or below 2.5m; in protected areas, side-garden positions and structures far from the house face tighter controls.
rules.roof_rules: Single-storey, low-key forms are the safest route. A dual-pitched roof can reach 4m, other roofs 3m, and roof terraces, raised platforms or overly domestic roof forms can push the room outside ordinary permitted development.
rules.materials_rules: Keep the room clearly ancillary to the main house. Large glazing areas and cladding can work, but the space should not be fitted out or used as self-contained accommodation with bedroom, bathroom and kitchen facilities operating as a separate unit.
